correctness.rationale: For each tangent line, direct solution of the ellipse intersection quadratic gives the exact formula \(L_A^2/4=(\alpha-r^2D)/\alpha^2\). Equality of two functions homogenizes to a sextic identity. A noncircular positive quadratic form has two distinct non-isotropic complex zero lines; restricting the sextic identity to each line forces the other quadratic form to share both factors and hence be proportional. Exact substitution yields \(k(k-1)\alpha^3=0\), so the factor is \(k=1\). The circular case reduces to equality of \(1/a-r^2\). All hypotheses, the strict-containment boundary, and both branches are explicit; no finite experiment is used as proof.

The published record “Global Barker–Larman rigidity for ellipsoids” states its theorem for every \(n\ge3\), with arbitrary ellipsoid center, and therefore has disjoint dimension from the present planar result.

originality.rationale: The 2001 source poses the general tangent-section reconstruction problem and reports partial results. The 2016 full-text local theorem covers sufficiently small smooth perturbations and quotes the classical constant-chord circle case, but does not yield global uniqueness for arbitrarily eccentric centered ellipses. The 2023 full-text survey still states the planar equal-tangent-chord problem as open in general. A published 2026 result proves global ellipsoid rigidity for dimensions \(n\ge3\), explicitly excluding the planar case. Exact-object, quadratic-form, tangent-chord, alias, and implication searches found no prior global planar centered-ellipse theorem.
residual_risks: The full original 2001 article was not available in the lawful public sources inspected, so an unindexed centered-ellipse lemma inside that article cannot be excluded from direct whole-document inspection alone.
An older tomography or conic-reconstruction source may phrase the same centered-ellipse result without Barker–Larman terminology.
The 2026 higher-dimensional ellipsoid result was compared at its published statement and summary level; its stated theorem excludes dimension two, though its proof techniques may be adaptable.

value.rationale: The theorem addresses a natural complete quadratic subclass of a published planar reconstruction problem. The centered ellipses form the full three-parameter centrally symmetric conic family, and the result extends beyond the known local perturbative regime to all admissible eccentricities. The exact factor mechanism is structural and reusable; this is not a renaming, arbitrary finite slice, or table recomputation.
